scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Lipsi was created in 1959 in East Germany by dance teachers Christa and Helmut Seifert as a communist alternative to Western rock and roll.
Promoted by the SED regime as a socialist social dance free of capitalist influence, it was officially introduced at a conference in Lauchhammer and patented worldwide by the state.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Lipsi was commissioned and deployed entirely as a political instrument of the East German state to shape youth culture and discourage Western influence.
It served as a propaganda tool during state-sanctioned balls, cultural conferences, and ideological campaigns until public rejection rendered it obsolete.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The Lipsi is a partner dance set in a 6/4 meter that begins in a classic ballroom hold.
The basic movement combines chassé steps, half-turns in waltz steps, and turns on both feet, incorporating figures from traditional folk dances such as the Ländler and Spinnradl.
The man controls turns and leans, while the woman executes stylized movements, including a traditional pose where she stands behind the man and looks over her shoulder.
Watch for Spinnradl Glance.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music for the Lipsi was recorded by East German ensembles such as the Rundfunk-Tanzorchester Leipzig and vocalists like Helga Brauer, released on the Amiga label.
It features a 6/4 time signature designed to offer a steady, controlled alternative to syncopated Western rhythms.
Listen for the dance orchestra instrumentation.
The pulse is 6/4.

A mid-century orchestral dance sound in 6/4 time featuring steady rhythms, brass and string arrangements, and clean German pop vocals intended to provide a predictable, unsinful alternative to rock and roll.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Christa and Helmut Seifert created the dance.
Helga Brauer was its best-known interpreting vocalist.

The dance was conceived primarily in Leipzig (derived from the Latin 'Lipsia'), with variations presented under titles like the Messe-Lipsi, but it failed to establish regional sub-genres due to its rapid public rejection and short lifespan.

The Lipsi traces its conceptual lineage to state-mandated socialist social dance directives in East Germany, drawing technical inspiration from traditional European folk dances like the Spinnradl and Ländler while opposing the lineage of American rock and roll.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Lipsi is influence of Spinnradl: Provided specific figures such as the woman standing with her back to the man and looking over her shoulder.
Lipsi is influence of Ländler: Contributed traditional folk elements integrated into the ballroom steps.
Lipsi is sibling of Berolina: Another newly invented East German propaganda dance from the same era.
